document.title: Comments of the PJM Cities and Communities Coalition re the PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms Technical Conference
document.group: PJM governance and stakeholder reform vote

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA ​
BEFORE THE ​
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION  
Commission-Led Technical Conference on PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms​
Docket No.  AD26-7-000 
COMMENTS OF THE PJM CITIES AND COMMUNITIES COALITION 
The PJM Cities and Communities Coalition respectfully submits these written 
comments in connection with the Commission-led technical conference on PJM 
Governance and Stakeholder Reforms in Docket No. AD26-7-000.  We applaud the 
Commission’s focus on governance issues within PJM, and we hope to aid the 
Commission’s investigation into these matters via the comments below.  
About PJMCCC 
The PJM Cities and Communities Coalition (PJMCCC) is a group of 21 local 
governments representing ~15% of the population within PJM's territory. Our members 
are energy managers and sustainability staff of large municipal end-users. 
As local governments, PJMCCC members are both large end-use consumers of 
energy and public-sector entities responsible for the health and well-being of our 
communities. This dual role places us in a unique position: we are affected by the 
impacts of PJM’s energy market decisions on our bills while being directly accountable 
to our approximately ten million residents who depend on reliable and affordable 
electricity. Furthermore, local government policy goals depend in part on consideration 
in PJM’s planning and decision-making so that the technologies and strategies needed 
to meet our mandates and goals are appropriately valued by markets.   
PJMCCC’s interests are unique and are not fully represented by any other 
stakeholder group, making our coalition a valuable partner in planning for PJM. For 
example, we are currently collaborating with PJM’s State Policy Solutions team to 
shape the development of the local policy portal to support PJM’s compliance with 
FERC Order 1920. We have been helping inform the policy fields to be used for 
aggregating local government policies, goals, siting opportunities, and siting restrictions. 
Additionally, we submitted local building and vehicle electrification objectives to PJM’s 
Load Analysis Subcommittee that were used in the 2024 load forecast. 
PJM is at a critical juncture, and decisions made now will be felt for decades to 
come. We strongly believe that local government policies and perspectives are crucial 
for ensuring that the future energy system is reliable, affordable, and sustainable.

PJMCCC members’ experience with PJM 
 
PJMCCC’s members’ experience attempting to interface with the PJM board via 
PJM staff has been, at best, a struggle.  While PJMCCC members have had an 
occasional successful encounter with PJM staff, these seem to be driven mostly by 
regulatory requirements rather than genuine efforts to facilitate constructive dialogue.  
PJMCCC did have a successful on-site meeting with PJM staff in 2023, but since then 
PJM staff has shown limited receptivity to outreach from PJMCCC.   
PJM staff have been difficult to get hold of when requesting tours at PJM 
headquarters in Pennsylvania, for example.  Routine difficulties getting hold of PJM 
customer service presented themselves. Once we did get in contact with staff over the 
phone, they mentioned that the email information on PJM’s website was inaccurate.  
Where PJM staff have opted to engage with PJMCCC members, it has primarily 
been where they are required to do so – for example, to facilitate PJM’s compliance with 
Order No. 1920.  PJM staff have contacted PJMCCC sporadically with asks for 
engagement and assistance on Order No. 1920 implementation.  One PJMCCC 
member aptly characterized the relationship to PJM as “don’t call us, we’ll call you.” 
The realm of the possible: FERC authority, State authority, and 
PJM politics 
PJMCCC is excited to see FERC take proactive steps toward exercising its 
authority over RTO/ISO governance, particularly with respect to PJM. While FERC has 
long held authority over RTO/ISO governance, many issues with RTO/ISO governance 
have persisted without FERC action.1  The time for FERC to use its authority to address 
pervasive issues in RTO/ISO governance, particularly within PJM, is nigh. 
 
FERC established minimum “independence” standards for RTO governance in 
Order No. 20002 and Order No. 719.3  As Travis Kavulla writes, “Independence” has 
been defined by FERC as having an ultimate decision-making body within an RTO that 
3 Federal Energy Regulatory Commission; “Wholesale Competition in Regions with Organized Electric 
Markets;” (October 17, 2008) Docket Nos. RM07-19-000, AD07-7-000. 
2 Federal Energy Regulatory Commission; “Order No. 2000: Regional Transmission Organizations;” 
(December 20, 1999) Docket No. RM99-2-000.  
1 Kavulla, T.; “Problems in Electricity Market Governance: An Assessment;” R Street Policy Study No. 
180; August 2019; 
https://www.rstreet.org/research/problems-in-electricity-market-governance-an-assessment/

is not beholden to “market participants.”4  A major test of FERC’s assertion of the 
authorities it has via its independence criterion came when FERC attempted to find 
CAISO’s board selection process to be insufficient for meeting FERC’s independence 
criterion. FERC’s main premise for this was that California law required the governor of 
California to approve candidates for the CAISO board and that the state of California 
was also a major participant in CAISO markets.   
 
However, the DC Circuit for the Court of Appeals rejected FERC’s attack on 
CAISO’s board selection process, writing that FERC had no authority to prescribe how a 
CAISO selects its board.5  While the DC Circuit preserved FERC’s authority over 
governance - noting that FERC could legitimately revoke an RTOs’ certification as an 
RTO on governance independence grounds - the DC Circuit found that FERC had 
overreached with regards to CAISO.  The DC Circuit noted that FERC’s arguments had 
no limiting principle, meaning these arguments could imply that FERC has authority 
over matters as minute as how CAISO procures office furniture.  While the DC Circuit 
left the door open for FERC to pursue further governance actions in CAISO, FERC 
declined to do so. 
 
Despite CAISO v FERC, FERC has used its rates authority to assert authority 
over governance.  FERC used its rates authority to reject revisions to ISO-NE’s 
governance, specifically ISO-NE’s membership rules in the stakeholder process, stating 
that “stakeholder processes are a practice affecting rates.”6   FERC’s order on this was 
unchallenged.   
 
​
That FERC’s authority over governance has been left unchallenged is a good 
thing, given the plethora of governance problems pervasive in PJM and the current 
market crisis that has resulted.  PJM’s governance structure itself has multiple problems 
that compromise its ability to meet FERC’s independence standards for RTOs.  A key 
issue with PJM is that its board is not truly independent from its members, who are also 
market participants.  PJM’s board is selected by its members, which limits the 
independence of the board from the outset.  Further, even if the PJM board tries to be 
independent, PJM members have so much influence that they can stifle action from the 
PJM board.  PJM members can effectively nullify any independent action that the board 
6 Order Rejecting Revisions, New England Power Pool Participants Committee, Docket No. 
ER18-2208-001, Jan. 29, 2019, p. 19. https://elibrary.ferc.gov/idmws/file_list.asp?document_id=14740301 
5 California Independent System Operator v. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 372 F.3d 395, 403 
(D.C. Cir. June 22, 2004); https://caselaw.findlaw.com/court/us-dc-circuit/1344700.html 
4  Kavulla, T.; “Problems in Electricity Market Governance: An Assessment;” R Street Policy Study No. 
180; August 2019; 
https://www.rstreet.org/research/problems-in-electricity-market-governance-an-assessment/

tries to take through the voting process and through the stakeholder issue 
agenda-setting process.  This is a serious problem for the PJM board, to the extent that 
the PJM board can’t arguably be said to control what happens in PJM.  
 
A further governance challenge is that PJM’s stakeholder process has become 
compromised as well.  As law professor Shelly Welton explains, the congressional 
repeal of the Public Utility Holding Companies Act (PUHCA) has allowed for swaths of 
mergers within the utility industry.7 This has resulted in merging together entities that 
once represented different sides of a transaction - creating problems for the balances of 
interests that RTO governance might intend to create.  When a “load” stakeholder is 
owned by the same entity as a “generation” stakeholder, neither is truly representative 
of its interests in an RTO stakeholder process. As professor Welton writes, these 
mergers “...create challenges by concentrating economic and political power in a small 
number of companies—not least for theories of RTO governance, which rely upon 
internal industry checks to legitimate RTO decision-making.  These internal checks 
presume opposing interests that do not exist because holding companies have 
consolidated across demand- and supply-side affiliates.”8  Professor Welton’s 
cross-RTO assessment of this issue holds true for PJM.  
 
As such, FERC’s authority over governance can be usefully deployed at this 
critical moment to resolve serious issues in PJM - and FERC should feel empowered to 
do so.  While there might be potential naysayers regarding FERC action toward PJM 
governance, FERC’s clear authority and rebuttals to these naysayers is neatly 
summarized in the following paragraph from law professor Ari Peskoe:  
 
“Should FERC impose governance reforms, opponents would likely argue that 
RTO governance is too ‘remote’ to directly affect rates, and that the [Supreme 
Court] did not hold that FERC’s authority extends beyond ‘rate structures.’ FERC 
could respond that the CAISO panel held only that FERC ‘does not have the 
authority to reform and regulate the governing body of a public utility.’ This 
holding is strictly limited to the facts of that case and does not limit FERC’s 
jurisdiction over governance matters that directly affect rates. FERC can also 
point to its orders about unduly discriminatory regional IOU alliances, as 
8 Welton, S.; “Rethinking Grid Governance for the Climate Change Era;” (2021) California Law Review; 
Vol. 109; pp. 237; 
https://www.californialawreview.org/print/rethinking-grid-governance-for-the-climate-change-era 
7 Welton, S.; “Rethinking Grid Governance for the Climate Change Era;” (2021) California Law Review; 
Vol. 109; pp. 234-237; 
https://www.californialawreview.org/print/rethinking-grid-governance-for-the-climate-change-era

summarized in part IV, to argue that there is nothing ‘unheralded’ or 
‘transformative’ about its regulation of RTO governance.”9  
 
Professor Peskoe even goes further to suggest that FERC could challenge and 
overturn the D.C. Circuit’s findings in CAISO v FERC: 
 
“FERC could also argue that the CAISO court’s policy arguments are irrelevant. 
The D.C. Circuit feared that if it upheld FERC’s order firing CAISO’s board, FERC 
might use that authority to hire and fire IOU board members.  The panel 
observed that other agencies, such as the Securities and Exchange Commission, 
regulate corporate governance, and that FERC authority over corporate boards 
would be redundant or even conflicting. But no such overlap would exist for RTO 
governance. FERC’s assertion over internal RTO decisionmaking structures and 
processes would not extend to analogous processes at IOUs. IOUs do not have 
‘members’ engaged in similar decisionmaking processes that directly affect 
FERC filings. Moreover, no other regulator can claim authority over RTO 
governance. This would be a winnable case for FERC.”10  
 
​
To aid FERC’s deployment of its governance authority, there is fortunately an 
abundance of literature suggesting a wide variety of reforms regarding RTO governance 
generally.11  Many of these reforms would be good solutions for PJM governance in 
particular.  This literature also includes recommendations for FERC to perform a more 
holistic revisitation of RTO/ISO governance, including explications of governance 
principles implicit in its prior orders and expansions of the governance principles FERC 
requires RTOs/ISOs to implement.12  Underscoring the need for governance reform, this 
literature also includes empirical demonstration that the governance structure of RTOs 
12 Simeone, C.E.; “Reforming FERC’s RTO/ISO Stakeholder Governance Principles;” The Electricity 
Journal, Vol 34 (2021); 
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1040619021000452?via%3Dihub 
11 See e.g. Lenhart, S., and Fox, D.; “Participatory Democracy in Dynamic Contexts: A Review of 
Regional Transmission Organization Governance in the United States;” Energy Research & Social 
Science; vol. 83 (2022); 
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2214629621004369?via%3Dihub  
10  Peskoe, A.; “Replacing the Utility Transmission Syndicate’s Control;” Energy Law Journal, Volume 
44.3, pp.612; 
https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Replacing-the-Utility-Transmission-Syndicates-
Control-FINAL.pdf 
9  Peskoe, A.; “Replacing the Utility Transmission Syndicate’s Control;” Energy Law Journal, Volume 44.3, 
pp.611-612; 
https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Replacing-the-Utility-Transmission-Syndicates-
Control-FINAL.pdf

can have profound impacts on market outcomes, specifically PJM’s governance 
capacity market.13  
 
In these comments, we attempt to focus only on literature that suggests reforms 
relevant to PJMCCC’s experience with PJM.  We note that other reforms beyond these 
might be valid and helpful, but we rely on other commenters to offer those reforms.  
 
Responses to Panel Questions 
Please find our responses to the panel questions below.  
Panel 1: PJM Governance Mechanics – Board Authority, States’ Role, Filing 
Rights, and Document Architecture 
1.​ What is the PJM Board’s role in ensuring that PJM is sufficiently tackling the 
region’s operational and market challenges?  How does the Board evaluate its 
effectiveness in that role?  How often, and under what circumstances, does the 
Board act unilaterally, and should this change? 
 
PJMCCC believes that the PJM board’s role is to make responsible decisions for 
the entire PJM region, including all stakeholders, rather than simply reflecting the 
preferences of member utilities. As such, PJMCCC believes that the PJM board should 
be made more representative of regional stakeholders and their interests. However, the 
PJM board is unlikely to become representative in this way under the current process 
used to select PJM board members. Under the current process, only PJM members 
vote to decide who sits on the PJM board - a process that can only guarantee that the 
PJM board will only represent PJM members and, more specifically, PJM member 
utilities that have the most voting power. This in turn sets up PJM to be led by a board 
that prefers policies favoring member utilities’ interests over other stakeholders and the 
public interest.  
 
Solution: 
PJM’s board selection process should be re-organized to require participation 
from stakeholders other than PJM Members.  PJM’s board selection process should 
include input from states, consumer advocates, and other stakeholders so as to deliver 
a board that is representative not only of PJM member utilities but of the region’s many 
other stakeholder sectors as well.  This would deliver a board that is both representative 
13 Blumsack, S., and Yoo, K.; “RTO Governance Structures Can Affect Capacity Market Outcomes;” 
Proceedings of the 53rd Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences, 2020; 
https://hdl.handle.net/10125/64119

of, and responsive to, the region’s needs.  PJMCCC agrees with Jacob Finkel’s 
comments on behalf of the PJM Governors’ Collaborative, which provide more useful 
details on issues with independence of the PJM board and solutions to make the PJM 
board more independent.14 
 
Who would do it, under what authority, and how: 
FERC could facilitate change to PJM’s board selection process by issuing an 
order to show cause requiring PJM to demonstrate how its board selection process 
meets FERC’s independence requirements for RTOs.  FERC could preliminarily find 
that, by restricting the board selection process to member votes, PJM fails to retain its 
independence from market participants.  FERC could argue that literature 
demonstrating the vulnerability of PJM’s board to its members’ influence creates 
grounds for preliminarily finding that PJM’s board is not sufficiently independent to meet 
Order No. 2000’s requirements. However, in proposing a just-and-reasonable remedy, 
FERC should not mandate an alternative selection process for PJM’s board; instead, 
FERC could propose to reconsider whether PJM should keep its status as an RTO. 
 
FERC’s potential action here would accommodate the D.C. Circuit’s finding in 
CAISO v FERC (2004).15  Since board selection processes have been squarely 
identified by the D.C. Circuit as a practice that FERC cannot control under the Federal 
Power Act, FERC should avoid attempting to dictate a new process to PJM (even if PJM 
needs one).  Instead, FERC should take the path identified by the D.C. Circuit as 
squarely within its jurisdiction - challenging an RTO’s compliance with FERC’s 
standards for independence.  This avoids the challenge of establishing a new limiting 
principle for FERC’s authority over governance via its authority over rates. 
 
Alternatively, PJM could file with FERC under Federal Power Act section 205 to 
voluntarily re-organize its board selection process into one that allows votes from 
non-member stakeholders.  Models exist from which PJM could borrow, such as the 
Regional Organization for Western Energy (ROWE)’s process for board selection.16  
ROWE is being developed by western stakeholders to provide new governance for the 
16 See West-wide Governance Pathways Initiative; “Launch Committee Step 2 Final Proposal;” pages 
57-61;  
https://www.westernenergyboard.org/wp-content/uploads/Pathways-Initiative-Step-2-Final-Proposal.pdf 
15 California Independent System Operator v. Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 372 F.3d 395, 403 
(D.C. Cir. June 22, 2004). https://caselaw.findlaw.com/us-dc-circuit/1344700.html. 
14 “Pre-Technical Conference Statement: Jacob Finkel, Office of Governor Josh Shapiro, Deputy 
Secretary of Policy;” (July 16, 2026) Docket No. AD26-7-000. 
https://elibrary.ferc.gov/eLibrary/filelist?accession_number=20260716-4005&optimized=false&sid=140709
8d-e46c-4292-acf1-eb7310602cdc

Western Energy Imbalance Market (WEIM) and Extended Day-ahead Market (EDAM).17 
In that selection process, regulators from state public service commissions have an 
input on what candidates are chosen to serve on the ROWE board.  This allows for 
better representation of the ROWE’s regional stakeholders and, as such, has much 
greater potential to deliver good policymaking. 
 
2.​ How should states, through the Organization of PJM States, Inc. (OPSI) or other 
structures, interface with the Board to enable the region to meet operational 
and market challenges while respecting PJM’s independence?  
 
A better PJM governance structure would include mandatory, regular, and 
responsive check-ins with the states and other stakeholders on a broader variety of 
policy topics.  PJMCCC believes that PJM should have a dedicated and regular forum 
to allow non-member stakeholders to provide input on PJM policy issues.  PJMCCC 
believes that FERC is asking the right question when inquiring if states’ input should be 
reaching the PJM board, and FERC should ask a broader question about how other 
stakeholders reach the board as well.  
 
As with board selection, an example of how best to do broader stakeholder 
engagement from which PJM should borrow is that of the ROWE.  ROWE’s structure 
requires the ROWE board to consult with states and other non-utility stakeholders 
regularly.  PJM’s governance structure would benefit from a similar structure and a 
direct line of contact between the PJM board, on the one hand; and states and other 
stakeholders in the region, on the other hand. 
 
Who would do it, under what authority, and how 
FERC has a variety of options to initiate this kind of restructuring in the PJM 
stakeholder process.  FERC could direct the PJM board to hold such talks with states 
and other stakeholders under its general power to direct convenings (e.g. this tech 
conference, the FERC+states collaborative, etc.).  However, this approach is likely to 
put significant strain on FERC resources, especially considering the rapidly growing 
plethora of issues facing PJM.  As a less-intensive alternative, FERC could also employ 
17 The WEIM and EDAM are currently governed jointly by the California Independent System Operator 
(CAISO) and the Western Energy Market (WEM) governing board. See generally 
https://www.westernenergymarkets.com/governance/governing-body

a Federal Advisory Committee process to convene PJM board members with other 
stakeholders and discuss relevant issues.18   
As a third alternative, FERC could issue a show-cause order against PJM 
arguing that its tariffs are unjust and unreasonable for lack of better engagement with 
non-member stakeholders.  As with its uncontested order on ISO-NE’s membership 
requirements, FERC could assert that PJM’s stakeholder processes are a practice 
affecting rates.19  FERC could then preliminarily find that PJM’s stakeholder processes, 
particularly their lack of regular engagement with broader stakeholders, are leading to 
unjust and unreasonable rates.  FERC could refer to ample literature on incumbency 
bias created by governance structures like PJM’s as grounds for this finding.20  As a 
just-and-reasonable remedy, FERC could propose that PJM adopt more regular 
engagement with a broader array of stakeholders, such as the engagement processes 
proposed for the ROWE.  
  
3.​ What governance reforms would best improve accountability and 
responsiveness? 
 
​
PJMCCC believes that improving the accountability and responsiveness of PJM 
goes beyond the PJM board selection process and engagement with the states.  
PJMCCC sees further opportunity with the PJM stakeholder process to improve PJM’s 
responsiveness.  As noted by professor Peskoe, “In PJM, the board now routinely calls 
for staff-driven processes that bypass standard committee-led deliberative processes.”21  
Moreover, empirical analysis has found that PJM culture has changed over time to rely 
more heavily on these fast-track processes that circumvent the deliberative stakeholder 
21 Peskoe, A.; “Replacing the Utility Transmission Syndicate’s Control;” Energy Law Journal, Volume 44.3, 
pp.616; 
https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Replacing-the-Utility-Transmission-Syndicates-
Control-FINAL.pdf 
20 See generally.  Peskoe, A.; “Replacing the Utility Transmission Syndicate’s Control;” Energy Law 
Journal, Volume 44.3; 
https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Replacing-the-Utility-Transmission-Syndicates-
Control-FINAL.pdf 
19 Order Rejecting Revisions, New England Power Pool Participants Committee, Docket No. 
ER18-2208-001, Jan. 29, 2019, p. 19. https://elibrary.ferc.gov/idmws/file_list.asp?document_id=14740301 
18 For examples from other agencies’ use of this process - notably CFTC’s - see Kavulla, T.; “Problems in 
Electricity Market Governance: An Assessment;” R Street Policy Study No. 180; August 2019; 
https://www.rstreet.org/research/problems-in-electricity-market-governance-an-assessment/

processes.22  Legal scholars have offered a simple solution to this issue that is well 
within FERC’s authority.  
The solution 
 
As articulated by professor Peskoe, FERC could require PJM to provide 
non-member stakeholders with the authority to initiate deliberative stakeholder 
processes within PJM’s existing structure.  This would allow issues that reflect regional 
stakeholder concerns to be put on the PJM stakeholder agenda, instead of issues that 
only the member utilities believe is important.  FERC could require this change under its 
general authority over governance processes as a practice affecting rates, as described 
elsewhere in these comments.  
 
4.​ How does the division of Federal Power Act section 205[1] filing rights among 
PJM, Transmission Owners, and the Members Committee affect PJM’s ability to 
act effectively and quickly, when warranted, to address operational and market 
needs? 
 
PJMCCC believes 205 filing rights are a key component of making PJM more 
responsive to regional stakeholders’ concerns.  The allocation of 205 filing rights 
currently stifles PJM board action and mainly facilitates a meager level of independence 
and responsiveness through the PJM board’s ability to file a 206 investigation against 
PJM itself.  This is obviously less than ideal for facilitating PJM reforms and also reflects 
the failure of PJM’s governance structure to create pathways for the PJM board to be 
responsive to regional stakeholders’ concerns.  
The solution 
 
PJMCCC believes that FERC should broaden the allocation of 205 filing rights in 
line with professor Peskoe’s recommendations.23 After the Atlantic City v FERC 
decision, FERC promised to investigate the allocation of 205 filing rights if utilities use 
those rights in a way that compromises RTO independence or causes undue 
23 Peskoe, A.; “Replacing the Utility Transmission Syndicate’s Control;” Energy Law Journal, Volume 44.3, 
pp.614-616; 
https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Replacing-the-Utility-Transmission-Syndicates-
Control-FINAL.pdf 
22Johnson, N., Lenhart, S., and Blumsack, S.; “The Evolution of Participatory Policymaking for Regional 
Power Grids;” Energy Law Journal; Vol. 44; pp. 533-546 (2023). 
https://scholarworks.boisestate.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1169&context=pubadmin_facpubs

discrimination.24  On that note, law professor Joshua Macey has noted that “Utilities use 
their filing rights both to propose favorable market rules and to design governance 
structures that allow them to control the multi-member organizations that plan grid 
infrastructure and ensure resource adequacy.”25  Given issues with the responsiveness 
and independence of RTOs generally and PJM in particular, and the role that filing rights 
have played in that unresponsiveness, FERC could now follow through on its 
post-Atlantic promise. 
 
PJMCCC believes that FERC should consider broadening the allocation of 205 
filing rights. FERC could consider giving the PJM board independent 205 filing authority 
over topics like regional cost allocation and local planning. FERC could also consider 
allocating 205 filing rights to state regulators, who are ultimately responsible for setting 
the retail rates through which all investments are ultimately recovered.  State regulators 
with 205 filing rights could help represent the interests of broader stakeholders in PJM 
tariff changes.  It is worth noting that state regulators in MISO and SPP already have 
205 filing rights over transmission cost allocation and resource adequacy.  Given PJM’s 
struggles with resource adequacy, as evidenced by its extreme capacity market prices 
in recent years, giving 205 filing rights over resource adequacy to PJM state regulators 
is well worth FERC’s consideration.   
 
PJMCCC believes it would also be helpful for FERC to consider another remedy 
offered by professor Peskoe - requiring PJM to create a new stakeholder group 
centered around innovation and new technologies.26  FERC could then grant that 
stakeholder group 205 filing rights in order to empower the PJM governance process to 
make tariff reforms that facilitate innovation and new technologies.  PJMCCC agrees 
with professor Peskoe that enabling PJM to be more self-improving in this regard could 
be an even better path than the rulemaking processes FERC has engaged in thus far to 
accommodate new technologies.

44.3, pp.615-616; 
https://eelp.law.harvard.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/10/Replacing-the-Utility-Transmission-Syndicates-
Control-FINAL.pdf 
25 Macey, J; “Outsourcing Electricity Market Design;” University of Chicago Law Review, Vol 91, pp. 
1243:1330, https://chicagounbound.uchicago.edu/uclrev/vol91/iss5/1/ ​
 
24 Atlantic City Elec. Co., et al. v. FERC, 295 F.3d 1, 9‒11 (D.C. Cir. 
2002).https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/appellate-courts/F3/295/1/597196/

5.​ To what extent do provisions in PJM’s Operating Agreement, Transmission 
Owner Agreement, Open Access Transmission Tariff, Reliability Assurance 
Agreement, or Manuals impede timely decision-making by PJM?  
 
While PJMCCC leaves it to others to comment on opportunities to reform PJM’s 
governing documents, PJMCCC believes that such reforms would add more value if 
suggested actions for FERC described elsewhere in these comments were adopted.  
 
6.​ Recognizing regional differences, are there lessons from other regional 
transmission organization/independent system operator (RTO/ISO) governance 
structures that PJM could reasonably adopt to improve its responsiveness to the 
region’s operational and market challenges? 
 
PJMCCC recommends that FERC and PJM should consider the new ROWE 
governance model being promulgated by western stakeholders as an example of best 
practices for improving PJM’s responsiveness to the region’s challenges.27  The 
ROWE’s governance model includes several provisions that will make the ROWE more 
responsive to regional issues and stakeholder concerns, including: 
 
●​ ROWE board member selection by a wide array of stakeholders, including state 
regulators 
●​ A thorough process and structure for stakeholder engagement, including 
requirements for the ROWE board to conduct engagement with state regulators 
and consumer advocates 
●​ A balance of voting power that gives no stakeholder sector veto power over 
ROWE board decisions, making the ROWE boards actions truly independent 
●​ Concentration of 205 filing rights within the ROWE board  
​
PJMCCC encourages FERC to consider requiring PJM to enact some or all of 
the ROWE’s governance design features, many of which are specifically recommended 
elsewhere in these comments in response to the Commission’s particular questions.  
These features will lead PJM to be more responsive to the region’s challenges 
 
27 See generally West-wide Governance Pathways Initiative; “Launch Committee Step 2 Final Proposal;” 
pages 57-61;  
https://www.westernenergyboard.org/wp-content/uploads/Pathways-Initiative-Step-2-Final-Proposal.pdf

Panel 2: PJM Stakeholder Process – Design, Transparency, and Decision-Making 
1.​ Do sector-weighted voting and existing voting thresholds strike the right 
balance between achieving consensus and taking timely action?  
 
PJMCCC believes that non-utility stakeholders like local governments are 
underrepresented in the PJM’s stakeholder process.  Even if PJMCCC could become a 
member and vote in the process, PJMCCC would not have hardly any influence due to 
broader structural issues with PJM’s voting structure.  As described above, professor 
Welton explains how mergers and acquisitions have made the stakeholder sector 
definitions muddied when it comes to actually representing public interests.28   
 
The solution 
 
FERC should direct PJM to develop more cohesive sector formation and stricter 
requirements that a member must meet to join a sector, as well as a broader variety of 
sectors in order to represent stakeholder that currently aren’t eligible to become 
members.  In developing prescriptions for PJM’s stakeholder sector requirements, 
FERC could draw upon ROWE’s Stakeholder Representatives Committee design.  
ROWE’s design defines specific sectors and requirements that a member must have in 
order to vote with that sector.  Moreover, the sectors in ROWE’s design are broadly 
representative of a variety of stakeholders that PJM’s governance should aspire to 
represent as well.  
 
Who would do it, under what authority, and how 
As described for similar changes to the PJM stakeholder process, FERC could 
require PJM to make these changes under its own assertion that stakeholder processes 
are a practice affecting rates.  PJM could of course also voluntarily make these changes 
itself. 
 
2.​ What transparency reforms would improve the quality of PJM’s stakeholder 
process and increase stakeholder confidence in its decision-making? 
 
​
Professor Peskoe articulates that a general improvement in transparency, 
through a new FERC transparency principle, would improve RTO governance.

​
One potential implementation of this transparency principle would be for FERC to

solutions to make the PJM board’s meetings and decisions public to stakeholders.31

Showing the courage of our convictions, PJMCCC has made efforts to achieve

the development of the local policy portal to support PJM’s compliance with FERC

​
PJMCCC has also engaged with PJM’s Transmission Expansion Advisory 
Committee (TEAC), which has recently taken promising actions toward the kind of 
engagement necessary for all of PJM.  The leadership of PJM’s TEAC has taken

to allow more time for public stakeholders to raise questions and discuss issues in PJM 
transmission planning.  The TEAC leadership has also provided helpful details in 
response to questions about utilities’ local projects (i.e. supplemental projects).   
 
Importantly, the leadership of PJM’s TEAC has made considerable efforts to keep 
the scope of discussion at TEAC meetings narrowed to PJM transmission planning, 
because stakeholders in the PJM region have many topics to discuss.  It is a fair 
assessment that stakeholders sometimes introduce topics that are outside the scope of 
TEAC meetings, but this is only a strong indication that PJM needs to expand its regular 
engagement with non-member stakeholders into other topic areas.  PJM should develop 
organizational routines and structures for similar engagement on all policy issues 
undertaken by PJM.

4.​ Do existing governing document provisions (e.g., Operating Agreement, 
Manuals) impede stakeholder decision-making and what changes could be 
made to address them? 
 
As indicated elsewhere in these comments, PJMCCC leaves it to other entities to 
opine on the opportunities for improving stakeholder decisions via the governing 
documents.  PJMCCC believes that such improvements would be exponentiated if 
combined with the reforms suggested elsewhere in these comments. 
 
5.​ What reforms to the stakeholder process could ensure PJM can meet the 
region’s challenges? 
 
​
Beyond the reforms outlined elsewhere in these comments, a further useful step 
would be for FERC to direct PJM to undertake the creation of an independent 
transmission monitor.34  An independent transmission monitor would be useful for 
providing review of the local transmission projects that are proposed by PJM utilities, 
which currently have no review and fall through a regulatory gap.  An independent 
transmission monitor would also be useful for ensuring consideration of 
non-transmission alternatives, like advanced transmission technologies, that would 
improve the overall efficiency of the PJM grid while also improving the affordability of 
electricity for PJM residents.

Members take to improve speed in decision-making while preserving 
stakeholder input?

As indicated elsewhere in these comments, PJMCCC strongly believes that 
stakeholder input needs to be expanded at this juncture, rather than merely “preserved.”  
PJMCCC views a lack of effort on PJM’s part to gather and respond to non-member 
stakeholder input as a key factor in getting the PJM region into the crisis it faces today.  
Much of the contemporary discourse on PJM issues focuses on the PJM capacity 
market.  Empirical research has found that PJM governance influences PJM capacity 
market outcomes.35  So the assertion that PJM’s unresponsive governance has led to 
the capacity market crisis facing the region should come as no surprise.   
 
As such, PJMCCC believes that the crisis will be resolved primarily through 
expanding stakeholder input rather than expediting decisions.  To that end, PJMCCC 
refers the Commission to its recommendations elsewhere in these comments as to how 
stakeholder input and engagement could be expanded.  In addition, the PJMCCC refers 
the Commission to its earlier recommendations to reform the PJM board as a means of 
achieving both faster and more responsive decision-making from PJM.   
 
7.​ Are there elements of PJM’s committee structure that routinely contribute to 
delays?  Are there stakeholder processes or issues that could be expedited or 
changed to provide greater focus on key issues and allow faster or more 
unilateral action on others? 
 
​
PJMCCC refers the Commission to the reforms outlined elsewhere in these 
comments.  PJMCCC appreciates FERC’s attention to the delays and desire to expedite 
PJM decisions.  PJMCCC believes that expanding non-member stakeholder input will 
be just as useful as expediting PJM decision-making, to the resolution of PJM’s current 
challenges, if not moreso.​
 
8.​ Should PJM increase the use of fast-path or time-bound review procedures to 
expedite committee action on high-importance topics?

PJMCCC notes that PJM has increasingly used fast-path procedures to address 
recent issues.36  However, In some cases those procedures have failed to deliver 
consensus and timely decision-making, such as the large load interconnection CIFP 
proceeding in which no proposal received enough votes to pass.37  As such, PJMCCC 
views the use of fast-path procedures as creating a strong risk of failing to resolve the 
underlying problems with PJM governance.  PJMCCC believes that the use of fast-path 
procedures goes against developing successful strategies for improving PJM 
decision-making in the way that the Commission’s questions indicate would be 
desirable.  PJMCCC encourages FERC to consider the reforms outlined elsewhere in 
these comments as better alternatives for addressing issues in PJM, rather than 
encouraging PJM to increase its use of fast-path procedures.   
 
9.​ Recognizing regional differences, are there lessons from other RTO/ISO 
stakeholder processes that PJM could reasonably adopt to improve speed in 
voting processes and stakeholder representation? 
 
As indicated elsewhere in these comments, PJMCCC believes that the ROWE’s 
newly proposed independent regional governance structure would be a valuable model 
for PJM.  The ROWE’s governance structure builds on lessons learned from other forms 
of regional market governance and develops robust processes for avoiding some of the 
failures seen in those other forms.  The ROWE’s structure moves away from a 
utility-centric governance model and toward one that gives more power to states, 
ratepayer advocates, and other public interest groups to influence market policies.  
FERC should consider the governance features of the ROWE and require PJM to adopt 
some of them, as outlined elsewhere in these comments.  
 
Conclusion 
Again, we applaud the Commission’s focus on governance issues within PJM, and we 
hope these comments will be of use to the Commission’s investigation into these 
issues.  We thank the Commission for the opportunity to comment, and we look forward 
to the Conference and to hearing remarks from both the panelists and Commissioners.
